content:
Write a two-digit number, reverse it, add the two. The total always divides by 11 — every single time. Playing with Numbers turns that kind of magic into technique, and the IMO turns the technique into marks. Start by testing the ground. The free IMO Class 8 Playing with Numbers online test below asks 10 exam-pattern MCQs and scores them on the spot. Each explanation shows the intended one-minute route.

What the IMO asks from Playing with Numbers in Class 8

  • General form: writing ab as 10a + b and abc as 100a + 10b + c.
  • Reverse-and-add, reverse-and-subtract patterns.
  • Divisibility tests for 2, 3, 5, 9, 10 and 11.
  • Cryptarithms: letters standing for digits.
  • Missing-digit puzzles built on divisibility.

Key facts and formulas to revise first

  • ab + ba = 11(a + b) and ab − ba = 9(a − b) — the two engines of this chapter.
  • Divisibility by 9 follows the DIGIT SUM; by 10, only the last digit matters.
  • For 11, take the alternating sum of digits; 0 or a multiple of 11 passes.
  • abc − cba = 99(a − c) — three-digit reversals always leave a multiple of 99.

Mistakes that cost Olympiad marks

  • Treating ab in general form as a × b instead of 10a + b.
  • Testing divisibility by 3 with the last digit (that trick belongs to 2, 5 and 10).
  • Dropping the carry in a cryptarithm column and "solving" an impossible puzzle.

questions.q: The sum of a two-digit number and the number formed by reversing its digits is 132. If the tens digit is 8, what is the number?
questions.explanation: Let the number be 10a + b. Sum with reverse: (10a + b) + (10b + a) = 11(a + b) = 132, so a + b = 12. With a = 8, we get b = 4. The number is 84. Check: 84 + 48 = 132.

questions.q: A three-digit number formed by repeating a single non-zero digit three times (like 111, 222, ...) is always divisible by:
questions.explanation: Such a number has the form aaa = 100a + 10a + a = 111a. Since 111a = 111 x a, the number is always divisible by 111. Note that 111 = 3 × 37, so it is also divisible by 3 and 37.

The sum of three consecutive odd numbers is 177. What is the middle number?
questions.explanation: Let the three consecutive odd numbers be n - 2, n, n + 2. Their sum: (n-2) + n + (n+2) = 3n = 177, so n = 59. The three numbers are 57, 59, 61. Check: 57 + 59 + 61 = 177.
